name: Haya
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Haya (haya1250) is not in the catalog. Both title-keyword items were run down. (1) Byarushengo, Hyman & Tenenbaum 1976 'Tone, accent, and assertion in Haya' was OBTAINED: Hyman's Berkeley CV gives a USC GSIL URL for the whole SCOPIL 3 volume (image-only scan, 152 MB); it was downloaded to and pp. 185-206 were scanned (one tesseract at a time, 300 dpi) into bht1976_ocr/. The paper states that Haya has two tones H/L, no phonetic stress (no penultimate lengthening or pitch perturbation on all-L words, p. 191; 'no accentual feature which we can single out', p. 195), and only an abstract phrase-penultimate accent before the % boundary realised as H-L -> F-L and L-H -> H-H, plus H-lowering next to pause. This is the best first-hand statement for a stress catalog: tone language, no word stress, phrase-level penultimate tonal accent. The same CV URL pattern yielded SCOPIL 6 'Haya grammatical structure' (1977; 111 MB, saved), whose 'Preliminaries' sect. 2.3 (p. 5, scanned in scopil6_prelim_ocr/) restates the analysis; this closes the 'SOURCE-NAMED-UNREACHABLE' verdict recorded for that volume in (2) Philippson 1991/92 thesis 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale' (Paris 5, 542 pp.): theses.fr record says not accessible online; no HAL deposit, no Google Books or open copy found; only the abstract was read (typology of ~30 East African Bantu languages from full tone to penultimate demarcative stress). Whether it treats Haya is unverified; priority medium, library-print-only. Also re-read from the earlier pass: Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 (Google preview, p. 88 conclusion: accent-like properties, possible final foot before %), Rehse 1912 pp. 4-5 and Herrmann 1904 p. 151 (colonial 'Betonung' remarks = tone marking, superseded). Hyman 2007/2009/2017 PhonLab papers on file cite Haya as a non-culminative /H, Ø/ tone system with penultimate L% attraction, consistent with BHT.fr, HAL, Crossref, Google Books API, USC GSIL); Semantic Scholar was rate-limited. in the haya1250 folder was appended with every new file.

[p.57] there is a phrase boundary (%) in such cases to which the following tone rules are sensitive: (6) a. H-L -> HL-L / __ % b. new_statements.rule_in_words: Haya is a tone language (privative /H/ vs. toneless, default L); there is no lexical word stress. The only positional prominence effects are phrasal: at the end of an assertion phrase (%), a penultimate H becomes a HL fall and a final H is anticipated onto the penult, after which any H immediately before pause is lowered (and an utterance-initial augment H is lowered after pause). The authors treat these as accent-like properties of an otherwise tonal system and explicitly leave open a phrase-final disyllabic foot; Hyman (2007:674, open PhonLab report, saved) later states outright that 'Haya has a full tone system whose Hs are not obligatory, culminative, or metrical', and Hyman (2009:195) summarizes the 1976 analysis as a phrase-final L% 'drawn to the penult'. Haya is not reported to have Bantu-style penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; no metrical structure posited at word level.
new_statements.exceptions: The HL/anticipation rules are keyed to the % (assertion-final) boundary, not to pause: vocative-preceding nouns (omútí káto) undergo them without being prepausal; negative and 'marked' TAMs and nouns before possessives/adjectives undergo H-tone reduction instead (pp.57, 73, 78). LH rising tones created by very late rules (h-deletion, mu -> syllabic m) escape contour simplification (p.88).
new_statements.domain_note: Phrase/utterance level (end of assertion, pre-pausal), realized on the penultimate and final syllables of the phrase; citation forms of nouns therefore show at most one H or HL (e.g. o-mú-ti 'tree' from /ó-mu-tí/), which the authors warn is misleading about the word-level system (p.56 per snippet; Hyman 2007:665). Data represent E. R. Byarushengo's Haya (Bukoba area); dialect footnote (p.54 n.1) not visible in preview.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 describe the Haya of co-author E. R. Byarushengo (Bukoba area, Tanzania); the dialect footnote (p.54 n.1) was not visible in the preview. The two colonial-era sketches describe named varieties: Rehse 1912/13 describes 'Ruziba', the speech of Kiziba (the Ziba/Kiziba dialect of Haya), and Herrmann 1904 describes 'Lusiba', specifically the 'Bayossa' dialect of Kjamtwara (Kyamutwara), both within Glottolog haya1250. Both old sketches use 'Betonung/Ton' impressionistically for what modern work analyses as H tone (Rehse: position depends only on grammatical form, no rule statable; Herrmann: penult, antepenult or pre-antepenult, variable even within one speaker's sentence).

new_statements.quote: Many Bantu languages have a phrase-penultimate accent which usually lengthens the vowel of that syllable, and perhaps has some additional pitch and intensity effects. If we look at a Haya word such as [okugulu] 'leg', with all L tones, we note neither a lengthening of the penultimate vowel, nor any pitch perturbation suggesting an accent on that (or any other) syllable. However, both rule (4) and rule (6) have the effect of bringing more prominence to the penultimate syllable. Rule (4), it is recalled, changes a H to a F tone when it is in penultimate position. Rule (6) has the effect of transferring a H from final to penultimate position.
new_statements.citation: Byarushengo, Ernest Rugwa, Larry M. Hyman & Sarah Tenenbaum. 1976. Tone, accent, and assertion in Haya. In Larry M. Hyman (ed.), Studies in Bantu tonology (SCOPIL 3), 185-205. Los Angeles: Department of Linguistics, University of Southern California.
new_statements.locator: p. 191, sect. 2 ACCENT (supporting: p. 185 intro; p. 190 table (16); p. 195; p. 203 conclusion; p. 204 n. 9)
new_statements.reading: Haya is a two-tone (H/L) Bantu language with no phonetic word stress: an all-low word shows no penultimate lengthening and no pitch prominence on any syllable, and the authors say outright (p. 195) that there is no accentual feature they can single out. The only 'accent' is an abstract phrase-penultimate accent, assigned to the second syllable before the phrase boundary % (not the word), whose sole exponents are tonal: H-L becomes falling-L and L-H becomes H-H before %, and H is lowered adjacent to pause. For a word-stress catalog this reads as: tone language, no word-level stress; phrase-level penultimate tonal accent only. Byarushengo 1977 (Preliminaries, p. 5) restates the same analysis; Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 (p. 88) keeps it and leaves open a final bisyllabic foot before %. The 1904 and 1912 German 'Betonung' remarks (Herrmann: penult/antepenult, freely variable; Rehse: depends only on grammatical form) are impressionistic tone-marking and are superseded.

sources.note: Haya analysed as a restricted tone system (underlying H vs. zero, L filled in by default); earlier 'tonal accent' analysis abandoned (p.54). Surface falling tone only in penultimate position (p.55); before the % phrase boundary (end of assertion) H-L -> HL-L and L-H -> H-H, then any pre-pausal H is lowered and a post-pausal initial-vowel H is lowered (p.57); H anticipation before % is 'a property characteristic of accent'; authors 'leave open the possibility that the final two syllables before a % boundary constitute a foot' (p.88). No word-stress rule stated.

sources.quote: Der Ton kann auf der vorletzten, drittletzten und viertletzten Silbe ruhen; letzteres ist selten, dagegen die beiden ersten Betonungen gleichmäßig im Gebrauch, so, daß dieselbe Person dasselbe Wort womöglich im selben Satz einmal auf der vorletzten und gleich darauf auf der drittletzten Silbe betont. Wenn in dem folgenden Wörterverzeichnis der Ton meist auf der vorletzten Silbe markiert ist, so geschah dies, weil es der Eigentümlichkeit der meisten ostafrikanischen Bantusprachen entspricht; die Betonung auf der drittletzten Silbe scheint mir mehr eine importierte Angewohnheit der Bahūma zu sein.
sources.note: Translation: 'The accent can rest on the penultimate, antepenultimate and pre-antepenultimate syllable; the last is rare, whereas the first two accentuations are equally in use, so that the same person may accent the same word, possibly in the same sentence, once on the penultimate and immediately afterwards on the antepenultimate. If in the following vocabulary the accent is mostly marked on the penultimate, this was done because it corresponds to the peculiarity of most East African Bantu languages; accentuation on the antepenultimate seems to me rather an imported habit of the Bahuma.' sources.quote: 2.3. Tone and accent. There are two underlying tones in Haya: high (H) and low (L). In addition there is a phrase-penultimate accent which causes a H-L sequence to become F-L (falling tone followed by low tone) and a L-H sequence to become H-H when occurring immediately before the % phrase boundary (cf. Byarushengo, Hyman and Tenenbaum 1976). Underlying H is converted to L before pause.
sources.locator: sect. 2.3 'Tone and accent', p. 5 (checked against page image)
sources.note: Grammar-sketch summary by a native-speaker linguist: Haya is a two-tone language; the only 'accent' is the phrase-penultimate accent of BHT 1976, defined purely by its tonal effects before the % boundary. No word-level stress is mentioned.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.
sources.note: Abstract only: a comparative typology of tone and penultimate accent across ~30 East African Bantu languages, from fully tonal (Kikuyu) to purely demarcative penultimate stress (Swahili), arguing that the rise of a penultimate demarcative accent drove the evolution of these systems. Whether Haya (JE22) is among the sample, and what it says about Haya, could not be verified; Hyman 2017 (already on file) cites Philippson 1991:193 only for Rundi-Rwanda.
